io-interface-001.question: Why have high-speed connections between chips and boards moved from parallel transmission over many wires to serial transmission over a few fast wires?
choices: In parallel transmission, arrival-time differences between wires (skew) make it hard to raise the speed
Serial transmission uses no electricity, so power drops to zero
Parallel transmission was banned by law
io-interface-001.explanation: Parallel transmission requires the bits on many wires to be captured together with one clock. As speed rises, arrival-time differences caused by tiny differences in wire length (skew) become significant compared with the clock period, so the speed cannot be raised further. Serial transmission recovers the clock from the data on each pair of wires, avoiding skew, so the speed per wire can be much higher. It also reduces the number of pins and traces.
choiceNotes: Correct. Fewer wires also mean less routing and fewer pins.
Serial links are electrical too and consume power.
It was never banned.

io-interface-002.question: What is the role of a SerDes (serializer/deserializer) in high-speed serial links?
choices: It encrypts data to prevent eavesdropping
It converts parallel on-chip data into one fast bit stream on the transmit side and restores the parallel data on the receive side
It converts supply voltages to suit other circuits
io-interface-002.explanation: Inside a chip, data moves slowly over buses dozens of bits wide. The SerDes transmitter reorders it into a single very fast bit stream, and the receiver recovers a clock from the stream, decides each bit and restores data of the original width. The physical layers of many high-speed interfaces, such as PCI Express, USB, Ethernet and storage links, are built from SerDes.
choiceNotes: It is not an encryption circuit.
Correct. It is the core circuit of serial transmit and receive.
It is unrelated to power conversion.

io-interface-003.question: Why do high-speed serial links use differential signaling, sending opposite signals on two wires?
choices: Two wires always double the amount of data sent
If one wire breaks, the other alone carries the data at the same speed
Noise picked up equally on both wires cancels when the difference is taken, so small swings can be sent fast and reliably
io-interface-003.explanation: In differential signaling, 0 and 1 are represented by the voltage difference between two wires. External noise couples almost equally onto the two closely routed wires, so it cancels when the difference is taken. This allows swings of only a few hundred millivolts, reducing the time and power needed to change voltage and enabling high speed. Because the two currents flow in opposite directions, electromagnetic emissions are also small.
choiceNotes: Two wires carry one signal, so throughput does not double.
One wire alone cannot be received as a differential signal.
Correct. It also emits less noise.

io-interface-004.question: What is the role of the clock and data recovery (CDR) circuit in a high-speed serial receiver?
choices: It amplifies a clock sent over a separate wire by the transmitter
It extracts clock timing from the transitions of the received data and decides each bit at that timing
It detects data errors and asks the transmitter to resend
io-interface-004.explanation: Sending the clock on a separate wire would introduce skew relative to the data. So in high-speed serial links, a CDR circuit watches where the data switches between 0 and 1, generates a clock of matching frequency and phase with a PLL or similar, and samples the data in the middle of each bit. This requires the data to contain transitions often enough, which line coding guarantees.
choiceNotes: Most high-speed serial links do not send the clock on a separate wire.
Correct. No dedicated clock wire is needed.
Retransmission is a higher layer's job.

io-interface-005.question: What has been the purpose of 8b/10b encoding (sending 8 data bits as a 10-bit code) in serial links?
choices: To compress data and reduce the amount sent
To balance the numbers of 0s and 1s and ensure frequent transitions so the receiver can recover the clock
To encrypt data so third parties cannot read it
io-interface-005.explanation: Long runs of 0s or 1s make the receiver's CDR lose timing and shift the average signal voltage, preventing correct decisions. 8b/10b encoding replaces 8 data bits with a 10-bit code that has nearly equal numbers of 0s and 1s and only short runs. The cost is 25% more bits on the wire, so data efficiency is 80%. It was used in PCI Express generations 1 and 2, USB 3.0 and others.
choiceNotes: The amount sent actually grows by 25%.
Correct. The goals are DC balance and guaranteed transitions.
It does not encrypt.

io-interface-006.question: On a link using 8b/10b encoding with a signaling rate of 5 Gb/s, what is the effective data rate?
choices: 4 Gb/s
5 Gb/s
io-interface-006.explanation: With 8b/10b encoding, 8 of every 10 bits sent are data, so the effective rate is 8/10 of the signaling rate: 5 Gb/s × 0.8 = 4 Gb/s. This is the one-direction speed of a single PCI Express 2.0 lane, or 500 MB/s in bytes. When comparing interfaces, the signaling rate (such as GT/s) and the coding efficiency must be considered separately.
choiceNotes: Correct. 5 × 8/10 = 4.
The extra coding bits must be subtracted.
That multiplies by 10/8, the wrong way round.

io-interface-007.question: Which is closest to the efficiency of the 128b/130b encoding adopted from PCI Express 3.0 onward?
choices: About 80%
About 50%
About 98.5%
io-interface-007.explanation: 128b/130b encoding sends 128 data bits with a 2-bit header as 130 bits, so efficiency is 128/130 ≈ 98.5%, a big reduction in waste compared with 8b/10b's 80%. Transitions are ensured by scrambling the data (XOR with a fixed pseudo-random sequence) to mix 0s and 1s. This is why PCI Express 3.0 nearly doubled effective throughput while raising the signaling rate only from 5 to 8 GT/s.
choiceNotes: 80% is the efficiency of 8b/10b.
The efficiency is far better than that.

io-interface-008.question: Which describes a "lane" in PCI Express?
choices: A unit of connection with one differential pair each for transmit and receive; lanes can be bundled for more bandwidth
A single wire that alternates between sending and receiving
The physical length of the slot into which a PCI Express device is inserted
io-interface-008.explanation: One PCI Express lane consists of a transmit differential pair and a receive differential pair, four wires in all, and carries data in both directions simultaneously. Bundling lanes as x4 or x16 spreads data across the lanes, so bandwidth grows in proportion to the lane count. Graphics cards commonly use x16, SSDs x4 and network cards x1 to x8.
choiceNotes: Correct. Lanes are bundled as x1, x4, x16 and so on.
Transmit and receive use separate pairs at the same time (full duplex).
Slot length corresponds to lane count but is not the lane itself.

io-interface-009.question: What is closest to the effective one-direction bandwidth of a PCI Express 3.0 x16 link (8 GT/s per lane, 128b/130b encoding)?
choices: About 128 GB/s
About 1 GB/s
About 16 GB/s
io-interface-009.explanation: The effective rate of one lane is 8 Gb/s × 128/130 ≈ 7.88 Gb/s, or about 0.985 GB/s after dividing by 8. Sixteen lanes give about 15.8 GB/s, roughly 16 GB/s in one direction, or about 32 GB/s for both directions together. PCI Express bandwidth is the product of the generation's per-lane rate, the coding efficiency and the lane count. Packet headers and other overhead make the real figure somewhat lower.
choiceNotes: The bits were not converted to bytes.
That is the bandwidth of a single lane.
Correct. About 0.985 GB/s per lane times 16.

io-interface-010.question: For PCI Express generations 3 through 6, how does the per-lane signaling rate change with each generation?
choices: It roughly doubles each time (8 → 16 → 32 → 64 GT/s)
It grows slowly by about 1.1× each time
The rate stays the same; only the lane count grows
io-interface-010.explanation: PCI Express signaling rates have roughly doubled each generation: 8 GT/s for Gen 3, 16 GT/s for Gen 4, 32 GT/s for Gen 5 and 64 GT/s for Gen 6. With bandwidth doubling for the same lane count, the interface keeps up with faster GPUs, SSDs and networks. Generations are compatible, so a new device in an older slot runs at the speed both support.
choiceNotes: Correct. Bandwidth doubles each generation.
It grows much faster than that.
The per-lane rate rises.

io-interface-011.question: What is a characteristic of PAM4 (four-level pulse amplitude modulation), adopted in PCI Express 6.0?
choices: It sends 1 bit per symbol using two voltage levels for 0 and 1
It sends 2 bits per symbol with four voltage levels, doubling the bit rate at the same symbol rate
It works only over optical fiber, not copper
io-interface-011.explanation: Conventional NRZ uses two voltage levels to send 1 bit per symbol. PAM4 uses four levels to represent 00, 01, 10 and 11, sending 2 bits per symbol. Channels attenuate signals more at higher frequencies, so doubling the bit rate without raising the symbol rate is the advantage. PCI Express 6.0 reached 64 GT/s with PAM4 at the same symbol rate as Gen 5.
choiceNotes: That describes NRZ (two-level signaling).
Correct. It raises speed without raising frequency.
PCI Express uses it over copper.

io-interface-012.question: Why does forward error correction (FEC) become more important with PAM4 than with NRZ?
choices: PAM4 makes clock recovery impossible, so every bit is wrong
Fitting four levels into the same swing shrinks the spacing to about one third, so noise causes more bit errors
PAM4 signals are encrypted and decryption errors must be fixed
io-interface-012.explanation: With the same voltage swing, two-level NRZ has the full swing between 0 and 1, but four-level PAM4 leaves only about one third of it between adjacent levels. The noise margin drops by roughly 9.5 dB, so bit errors become more likely. PCI Express 6.0 therefore adds a lightweight error-correcting code so the receiver can fix small errors before use.
choiceNotes: Clocks can be recovered with PAM4 too.
Correct. The noise margin shrinks.
It has nothing to do with encryption.

io-interface-013.question: What happens when an x4 PCI Express SSD is plugged into a full-length x16 slot on a motherboard (assuming the slot is wired for at least x4)?
choices: It does not fit, so it cannot be inserted
It works fine and connects with four lanes
It automatically expands to 16 lanes, quadrupling bandwidth
io-interface-013.explanation: In PCI Express, at the start of a connection both sides determine the lane counts and speeds they can use (link training) and operate at the largest common configuration. An x4 card in an x16 slot runs with four lanes. Conversely, a long slot may be wired for only x4, in which case an x16 card also runs at x4. Generations work the same way, settling on the speed of the generation both support.
choiceNotes: A shorter card fits in a longer slot.
Correct. It runs at the lane count both sides support.
It cannot exceed the card's own lane count.

io-interface-014.question: Which statement about the structure of PCI Express is correct?
choices: All devices share one bus, and only one device can use it at a time
Devices connect to each other wirelessly
From the root complex on the CPU side, devices (endpoints) connect through switches in a tree of point-to-point links
io-interface-014.explanation: Old PCI had several devices share one bus and compete for access. In PCI Express, the root complex, connected to the CPU and memory, is the root; switches branch out, and every link is a point-to-point connection between exactly two devices. Each link has its bandwidth to itself, so adding devices causes less contention, and signal quality is easier to maintain.
choiceNotes: That is a shared-bus scheme like old PCI.
The connections are wired.
Correct. Each link is dedicated to two devices.

io-interface-015.question: How does communication in PCI Express work?
choices: Addresses and data are driven simultaneously on many separate wires
Read and write requests are sent as packets and handled in three layers: transaction, data link and physical
The CPU directly controls every bit of every transfer
io-interface-015.explanation: PCI Express sends memory reads and writes and configuration requests as packets (TLPs) with headers and data. The transaction layer forms packets, the data link layer adds error-detecting codes and confirms delivery, and the physical layer encodes them and sends them through the SerDes. To software it still looks like reading and writing memory addresses, as with old PCI, which preserves compatibility.
choiceNotes: That is how a parallel bus works.
Correct. It has a layered structure like a network.
The CPU does not handle individual bits.

io-interface-016.question: What does the PCI Express data link layer do about bit errors during transmission?
choices: It does nothing and passes the data on until software notices
It powers off the device when an error is found
It adds a CRC to detect errors and, on error, signals that the packet was not received so it is resent
io-interface-016.explanation: The data link layer sends each packet with a sequence number and a CRC (cyclic redundancy check) code. The receiver checks the CRC and returns ACK if it is good or NAK if it is not; the sender keeps each packet until it is acknowledged and resends it on NAK. Thanks to this, even when the physical layer occasionally flips a bit, the upper layers and software receive correct data.
choiceNotes: The data link layer detects and recovers errors.
It does not cut power.
Correct. It is retransmission based on ACK and NAK.

io-interface-017.question: How are the registers and memory of a PCI Express device made accessible to the CPU?
choices: At boot the OS or firmware reads the size each device requests and assigns an address in its BAR (base address register), making it visible as memory addresses
Each device has a fixed address set at manufacture
The CPU cannot read device registers; everything goes through DMA
io-interface-017.explanation: A PCI Express device reports the sizes of its registers and memory through its BARs. At boot, the firmware or OS examines every connected device (enumeration) and assigns addresses so they do not collide. Afterward the CPU operates the device by reading and writing those addresses like ordinary memory. A device plugged in later is assigned addresses the same way.
choiceNotes: Correct. They are used as memory-mapped I/O.
Fixed addresses would collide between devices.
The CPU reads and writes registers directly.

io-interface-018.question: What is a characteristic of MSI (message-signaled interrupts) used in PCI Express?
choices: The device phones the CPU on every interrupt
No interrupts are used; the CPU continuously polls the device
The device signals an interrupt by writing to a designated address, so no dedicated interrupt wire is needed
io-interface-018.explanation: Older devices had dedicated interrupt wires, sometimes shared among several devices. With MSI, the device writes a designated value to an address set by the OS, and that write arrives at the CPU as an interrupt. Without the limit on wires, a device can have many interrupts; a network card, for example, can send a separate interrupt for each receive queue to a different core.
choiceNotes: Of course no telephone is involved.
That is polling.
Correct. Interrupts are sent as packets too.

io-interface-019.question: What is the difference between bandwidth and latency in interface performance?
choices: Bandwidth and latency are the same thing in different units
Larger bandwidth always means smaller latency
Bandwidth is the amount of data sent per unit time; latency is the time for one piece of data to arrive
io-interface-019.explanation: Bandwidth is like the number of lanes on a road, and latency like the travel time to the destination. More lanes let more cars through at once but do not shorten the time for one car to arrive. Large transfers are governed by bandwidth, while many small back-and-forth exchanges are governed by latency. Identifying which one dominates is the first step to improving performance.
choiceNotes: They are different quantities.
A link can have large bandwidth and still high latency.
Correct. They are different quantities and must be considered separately.

io-interface-020.question: On a link with 10 GB/s bandwidth and 1 µs latency, roughly how long does it take to send 64 bytes once (time = latency + size ÷ bandwidth)?
choices: About 6.4 ns
About 1 µs
About 101 µs
io-interface-020.explanation: 64 bytes ÷ 10 GB/s = 6.4 ns, so the time is 1 µs + 0.0064 µs ≈ 1 µs, nearly all latency. Sending 1 MB instead takes 100 µs + 1 µs ≈ 101 µs, determined almost entirely by bandwidth. When sending many small pieces, more bandwidth does not help, so the remedies are batching the data or using a lower-latency link.
choiceNotes: That is the transfer time alone, without latency.
Correct. It is almost entirely latency.
That is close to the time for 1 MB.

io-interface-021.question: Which is most effective for speeding up a program that exchanges thousands of small pieces of data with a device one at a time?
choices: Only switch to a link generation with twice the bandwidth
Batch the data into large chunks to reduce the number of exchanges
Split each piece into even smaller parts
io-interface-021.explanation: Each small exchange incurs latency and software overhead while leaving the bandwidth mostly idle. Sending the data together in one go pays latency fewer times and uses the bandwidth effectively. Storage and networking use the same idea widely, for example by queuing several requests and submitting them at once, or by coalescing interrupts.
choiceNotes: With small data latency dominates, so the gain is small.
Correct. Latency is paid fewer times.
More exchanges make it even slower.

io-interface-022.question: Which statement about how USB communication works is correct (for conventional USB, excluding USB4)?
choices: The host schedules communication and queries devices, which send data as the host directs
All devices are peers and can send data whenever they like
Devices normally communicate directly without the host
io-interface-022.explanation: In USB, the host, such as a PC, manages connected devices and decides which device to talk to and when. Even a mouse returns its input only when the host polls it periodically. This keeps devices simple, so many can be made cheaply. When plugged in, a device tells the host what kind it is, and the host loads a matching driver.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is host-driven.
Devices cannot send on their own initiative.
Communication is basically between host and device.

io-interface-023.question: Which statement about USB Type-C is correct?
choices: Any USB Type-C cable always communicates at the maximum speed
USB Type-C cannot be used to supply power
It is a connector-shape standard that plugs in either way up; the data rate is set by separate specifications
io-interface-023.explanation: USB Type-C is a standard for a small connector that plugs in either way up. Behind the same connector, the data link ranges from USB 2.0's 480 Mb/s to tens of Gb/s with USB 3.x or USB4, depending on what the cable and both devices support. It is also used for power delivery and video output, so cables and ports that look the same may differ in what they can do.
choiceNotes: Speed depends on the specifications the cable and devices support.
It can deliver substantial power via USB PD and similar.
Correct. Shape and speed are separate matters.

io-interface-024.question: Which describes USB Power Delivery (USB PD)?
choices: The source and sink negotiate voltage and current so that higher voltages than 5 V can deliver more power
It carries USB data over power lines
It always applies 20 V to every device to charge faster
io-interface-024.explanation: Basic USB power is 5 V with limited power. With USB PD, after connection the two sides communicate over the CC wire and agree on a voltage and current the sink can accept before the voltage is raised. It is used to charge laptops and similar, and extended versions can deliver up to 48 V at 5 A (240 W). Until the agreement is made, the supply stays at a safe 5 V.
choiceNotes: Correct. The latest version handles up to 48 V and 240 W.
It is not a power-line communication standard.
Applying a high voltage without negotiation would damage devices.

io-interface-025.question: Among USB transfer types, what is characteristic of isochronous transfers?
choices: They retry on any error to guarantee correct delivery; used for file transfers
They reserve bandwidth and send at fixed intervals but do not retry on error; used for audio and video
They are used only when configuring a device
io-interface-025.explanation: USB has control transfers for configuration, interrupt transfers for devices such as mice, bulk transfers for reliably moving large data and isochronous transfers for on-time delivery. In audio and video, data that arrives late is useless, so isochronous transfers reserve bandwidth, send at fixed intervals and do not resend on error. Smooth playback is prioritized over losing a little data.
choiceNotes: That describes bulk transfers.
Correct. It suits uses where a small gap beats a delay.
Configuration uses control transfers.

io-interface-026.question: Which describes hot plugging, supported by USB and some PCI Express setups?
choices: A function that automatically cuts power when a device gets hot
Devices can be connected and disconnected with power on, and the OS recognizes or detaches them automatically
A function that always reboots the computer when a device is plugged in
io-interface-026.explanation: Interfaces that support hot plugging protect devices during connection and removal with power on, using contact sequencing and current limiting, and the OS discovers new devices and loads drivers. Besides USB, it is used with PCI Express when swapping server SSDs, with SATA and others. Telling the OS before removal so that pending writes are completed is important for protecting data.
choiceNotes: That is a different, thermal protection function.
Correct. No reboot is needed.
Hot plugging means no reboot is needed.

io-interface-027.question: Which bus from Arm's AMBA specifications is widely used to connect blocks such as CPUs, memory controllers and peripherals inside an SoC?
choices: AXI
USB
SATA
io-interface-027.explanation: AXI (Advanced eXtensible Interface) is part of Arm's publicly available AMBA family of specifications and is widely used as the bus connecting blocks inside a chip. Following its signal conventions lets IP blocks designed by different companies connect to each other. Variants include high-performance AXI, the simple AXI4-Lite for register access and AXI4-Stream for data flows.
choiceNotes: Correct. It connects blocks inside a chip.
USB is an external standard for connecting devices.
SATA is an external standard for connecting storage.

io-interface-028.question: What is a characteristic of the AXI bus?
choices: It has five independent channels (read address, read data, write address, write data and write response) that can operate simultaneously
It sends addresses and data alternately on a single wire
Reads and writes can never occur at the same time
io-interface-028.explanation: AXI has five channels: read address (AR), read data (R), write address (AW), write data (W) and write response (B). Because they are independent, reads and writes can proceed at the same time, and addresses can be sent ahead of their data. Every channel uses the same VALID/READY handshake, giving a uniform design.
choiceNotes: Correct. Separate channels run in parallel.
It is a parallel bus with many wires.
Read and write channels are separate, so they can run together.

io-interface-029.question: In the VALID/READY handshake used on each AXI channel, when is data transferred?
choices: At a clock edge when both the sender's VALID and the receiver's READY are 1
The instant the sender sets VALID to 1, regardless of READY
The instant the receiver sets READY to 1, regardless of VALID
io-interface-029.explanation: The sender raises VALID when it has valid data, and the receiver raises READY when it can accept it; a transfer happens at a clock edge where both are 1. A busy receiver can hold READY low to make the sender wait (backpressure), so blocks of different speeds can connect without losing data. The rule that the sender must not wait for READY before asserting VALID prevents the two sides from waiting on each other forever.
choiceNotes: Correct. Transfer happens only when both agree.
The receiver cannot take data until it is ready.
Without valid data from the sender, nothing is transferred.

io-interface-030.question: What is the advantage of burst transfers in AXI?
choices: Data is compressed, reducing the amount sent
Each transfer rechecks the address, eliminating errors
One address covers several consecutive data items, reducing address overhead and using bandwidth effectively
io-interface-030.explanation: Data at consecutive addresses, such as a cache-line fill, is often handled together, so AXI can send just the starting address and a length and then stream the data as a burst. Not sending an address per item frees the address channel and keeps the data channel busy without gaps. DRAM is also good at burst reads and writes, so the two match well.
choiceNotes: It does not compress.
The benefit is omitting addresses, not rechecking them.
Correct. It suits reading and writing cache lines and similar.

io-interface-031.question: In AXI, what is the advantage of issuing the next read request without waiting for the previous one's response (having multiple outstanding requests)?
choices: Requests keep flowing during memory latency, hiding it and raising bandwidth
Fewer requests make the circuit smaller
Responses always come back in reverse order
io-interface-031.explanation: If each request waits for its response before the next is issued, with 100 cycles of memory latency the bus sits idle most of the time. AXI tags requests with IDs and allows several to be outstanding, so data keeps returning during the latency and bandwidth is used well. Requests with different IDs may complete out of order, so whichever finishes first can be returned first.
choiceNotes: Correct. IDs are used to tell them apart.
The number of requests does not decrease.
Ordering follows per-ID rules, not always reversed.

io-interface-032.question: What is AXI4-Lite mainly used for?
choices: Simple, low-volume exchanges such as reading and writing peripheral configuration registers
Moving huge volumes of data between a GPU and HBM
Connecting to external equipment by cable
io-interface-032.explanation: AXI4-Lite drops features such as bursts and multiple outstanding requests and simply reads or writes one data item at a time. Its small, easy-to-build circuits make it the usual way to connect the configuration registers of timers, communication blocks and the like to the CPU. Fast, high-volume transfers instead use full AXI or AXI4-Stream, which has no addresses.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is a simplified version without bursts.
Bulk transfers use full AXI with bursts or similar.
It is an on-chip bus.

io-interface-033.question: What is a characteristic of AXI4-Stream?
choices: It is for random reads and writes at specified memory addresses
It has no addresses and is meant for continuously streaming data in one direction, suiting video and signal-processing pipelines
It is a connector standard for external displays
io-interface-033.explanation: Circuits where data flows from stage to stage, such as video filters or communication signal processing, need no addresses. AXI4-Stream carries just data with the VALID/READY handshake, plus signals such as one marking the end of a packet, so data can flow continuously in one direction. It is also widely used in FPGA designs to connect processing blocks.
choiceNotes: Addressed access is what AXI and AXI4-Lite do.
Correct. Only data passes, with VALID and READY.
It is an on-chip specification.

io-interface-034.question: Why have large SoCs adopted a network-on-chip (NoC) instead of a single shared bus?
choices: A NoC enables wireless communication inside the chip
A shared bus carries only one transfer at a time, so it congests as blocks multiply and its wires grow long
The CPU cannot read memory over a shared bus
io-interface-034.explanation: A shared bus is enough with few blocks, but with dozens of CPU cores, GPUs and accelerators attached, a bus that carries one transfer at a time becomes congested. A NoC arranges routers and links in a mesh and sends data as packets along chosen routes, so many transfers between distant blocks travel simultaneously. Splitting wires into short segments also makes high clock frequencies easier.
choiceNotes: A NoC is also wired.
Correct. A NoC carries many transfers in parallel.
Memory can be read over a shared bus.

io-interface-035.question: Which describes CXL (Compute Express Link)?
choices: A standard for connecting chiplets inside a package
A standard that uses the PCI Express physical layer to allow coherent memory sharing between CPUs and accelerators or memory devices
A new wireless LAN standard
io-interface-035.explanation: With PCI Express, coherence between device memory and CPU caches is not maintained by hardware, so software had to take care of it. CXL runs on the same physical layer as PCI Express and adds protocols that maintain cache coherence and let the CPU read and write device memory like ordinary memory. It is used for sharing data with accelerators and for expanding memory.
choiceNotes: That is UCIe or similar.
Correct. It uses the same connectors as PCI Express.
It has nothing to do with wireless LAN.

io-interface-036.question: What is an advantage of memory expansion using CXL (CXL memory)?
choices: Latency is always lower than DRAM attached directly to the CPU
Data is always retained when power is off
Capacity can grow beyond the limit of the CPU's memory channels, and memory can be pooled among servers
io-interface-036.explanation: The memory attachable directly to a CPU is capped by its number of memory channels and slots. CXL memory adds capacity by attaching memory devices to PCI Express slots or similar, and with switches several servers can share pooled capacity. Its latency is higher than directly attached DRAM, though, so it is used as a tier, with frequently used data kept in direct memory.
choiceNotes: The longer path makes latency higher than directly attached DRAM.
The media is usually ordinary DRAM, not necessarily non-volatile.
Correct. It allows flexible expansion and sharing.

io-interface-037.question: Which correctly lists the three protocols that make up CXL?
choices: CXL.usb, CXL.sata and CXL.hdmi
CXL.read, CXL.write and CXL.erase
CXL.io (PCI Express-equivalent I/O), CXL.cache (device caches CPU memory) and CXL.mem (CPU uses device memory)
io-interface-037.explanation: CXL.io is essentially PCI Express traffic used for device discovery, configuration, interrupts and so on. CXL.cache lets an accelerator cache CPU-side memory in its own cache while keeping coherence. CXL.mem lets the CPU read and write device memory like ordinary memory. A memory-expansion device uses CXL.io and CXL.mem, while an accelerator may use all three.
choiceNotes: These are names of other external interfaces.
These sound like flash operations, not CXL protocols.
Correct. They are combined according to the use case.

io-interface-038.question: What is the role of equalizers (such as CTLE and DFE) in high-speed serial receivers?
choices: To adjust treble and bass to taste in music
To equalize the numbers of 0s and 1s in the data
To compensate for the channel attenuating high frequencies more, which smears the signal, and reduce inter-symbol interference
io-interface-038.explanation: Board traces and cables attenuate higher frequencies more, so a fast bit stream loses its sharp edges and remnants of earlier bits overlap later ones (inter-symbol interference). A CTLE boosts high frequencies to offset the loss, and a DFE estimates the overlap from bits already decided and subtracts it. The transmitter adds emphasis right after transitions (de-emphasis) as well.
choiceNotes: The name is shared with audio equipment, but the use differs.
That is the job of coding or scrambling.
Correct. It restores the shape of the smeared signal.

io-interface-039.question: Which statement about the eye diagram used to assess high-speed serial signal quality is correct?
choices: It overlays the waveforms of many bits; the wider and taller the central "eye" opening, the more margin there is
The more closed the eye, the better the signal
It is a chart for checking the health of human eyes
io-interface-039.explanation: An eye diagram slices the waveform at each bit period and overlays the pieces. An eye-shaped gap appears between the 0 and 1 traces; its height represents the margin against noise and its width the margin against timing variation (jitter). Channel loss, reflections and jitter close the eye. The receiver decides bits at the center of the eye, so its opening is a measure of quality.
choiceNotes: Correct. It shows margins against noise and timing jitter.
A closed eye makes 0s and 1s hard to tell apart.
It is a chart for evaluating electrical signals.

io-interface-040.question: Why does raising serial link speed make it harder to send signals over board traces of the same length, sometimes requiring retimers along the way?
choices: Trace loss grows with frequency, so faster signals are attenuated more over the same distance
Fast signals travel through traces faster than light
Faster signals make trace resistance approach zero and draw too much current
io-interface-040.explanation: In traces, conductor loss from the skin effect and dielectric loss from the board material both grow with frequency. Doubling the speed weakens the signal much more over the same length, beyond what the receiver's equalizer can recover. So designers use low-loss board materials or insert retimers that receive the signal and retransmit a clean copy.
choiceNotes: Correct. A retimer receives and retransmits the signal afresh.
Nothing travels faster than light.
Losses actually increase with frequency.

io-interface-041.question: What does a requirement of "bit error rate (BER) at most 10^-12" for a high-speed serial link mean?
choices: Up to 12 bit errors per second are acceptable
One bit in every 12 is wrong
On average no more than one bit in a trillion is wrong
io-interface-041.explanation: The bit error rate is the fraction of transmitted bits that are received incorrectly. 10^-12 means one bit in a trillion; on a 10 Gb/s link that is about one error every 100 seconds on average. Small as it looks, errors still occur fairly often at high speed, so PCI Express and others use data-link retransmission or error correction to keep errors from reaching upper layers.
choiceNotes: It is not a count of errors per unit time.
That error rate would make communication useless.
Correct. 10^12 is one trillion.

io-interface-042.question: Why are high-speed signal traces designed so that their characteristic impedance matches the transmit and receive circuits?
choices: To reduce trace resistance to zero and eliminate loss
To make traces glow so they can be checked visually
To prevent reflections at impedance discontinuities from distorting the waveform
io-interface-042.explanation: At high speed, a trace behaves as a transmission line along which electrical waves travel. Wherever the characteristic impedance changes, at connectors, vias or mismatched terminations, part of the signal reflects back and overlaps later bits, distorting the waveform. Designers therefore tune trace width and layer spacing so that, for example, differential traces are 100 Ω, and terminate them with the same value.
choiceNotes: Matching impedance does not remove resistive loss.
Traces do not glow.
Correct. Differential traces target values such as 100 Ω.

io-interface-043.question: High-speed links such as 100-gigabit Ethernet are sometimes built by bundling, for example, four 25 Gb/s lanes. Which describes this approach?
choices: Three of the four are spares; data actually travels on just one
The same data is sent on all four and errors are fixed by majority vote
Because per-lane speed is limited, data is spread across several SerDes lanes to reach the total bandwidth
io-interface-043.explanation: The speed of one SerDes lane is limited by circuit and channel technology. Spreading data across several lanes and realigning it in order at the receiver yields large total bandwidth. As per-lane speeds rise, the same bandwidth needs fewer lanes; for example, a single 100 Gb/s PAM4 lane can carry 100-gigabit traffic.
choiceNotes: All lanes carry data.
The data is divided, not duplicated.
Correct. It is the same idea as PCI Express lanes.

io-interface-044.question: What is the purpose of spread-spectrum clocking (SSC), used in PCI Express and elsewhere?
choices: To raise the clock frequency greatly and double the data rate
To vary the clock frequency slightly, spreading electromagnetic emission energy over a wider band and lowering its peak
To stop the clock and cut power to zero
io-interface-044.explanation: Circuits clocked at a fixed frequency emit sharp noise peaks at that frequency and its harmonics, which can exceed electromagnetic interference limits. SSC slowly sweeps the clock frequency up and down by about 0.5%, spreading the noise energy over neighboring frequencies and lowering the peaks. The receiver's CDR is designed to track this slow variation and still capture the data.
choiceNotes: The variation is about 0.5% and does not raise speed.
Correct. It makes electromagnetic interference limits easier to meet.
The clock is not stopped.

io-interface-045.question: What does it mean that a PCI Express lane is full duplex?
choices: It can transmit and receive simultaneously
It alternates between transmitting and receiving
It can only transmit, never receive
io-interface-045.explanation: Full duplex means data can flow in both directions at once. A PCI Express lane has separate transmit and receive differential pairs, so it can, for example, send data to a GPU while simultaneously receiving results back. This is why bandwidth figures must state whether they are per direction or a two-way total. Using one set of wires alternately is called half duplex.
choiceNotes: Correct. Transmit and receive use separate differential pairs.
That is half duplex.
It can receive too.

io-interface-046.question: Which describes the credit-based flow control used in PCI Express?
choices: The receiver advertises its free buffer space as credits, and the sender transmits packets only within those credits
The sender transmits regardless of the receiver, and overflowing packets are discarded
Users are billed according to the amount of data sent
io-interface-046.explanation: Sending a packet into a full receive buffer would waste effort in discarding and resending it. With credits, the receiver tells the sender how much more it can accept, the sender transmits only within that amount, and the receiver returns credits as it processes packets and frees buffer space. Overflow never occurs, so there is no discarding and resending.
choiceNotes: Correct. Buffers never overflow.
The mechanism exists precisely to prevent overflow.
It has nothing to do with financial credit.

io-interface-047.question: In AI systems with many GPUs, why are dedicated high-speed GPU-to-GPU links (such as NVIDIA NVLink) used in addition to PCI Express?
choices: PCI Express cannot connect even one GPU
A dedicated link makes GPU memory unnecessary
Training large models exchanges huge amounts of data between GPUs, needing more bandwidth than PCI Express
io-interface-047.explanation: When multiple GPUs train a large AI model, they frequently exchange gradients, parameters and intermediate results mid-computation. If this communication is slow, the GPUs stall waiting. Dedicated GPU-to-GPU links bundle many fast SerDes lanes so GPUs can exchange data directly with several times the bandwidth of PCI Express.
choiceNotes: GPUs normally connect via PCI Express.
GPU memory is still needed.
Correct. Inter-GPU communication easily becomes the bottleneck.

io-interface-048.question: In PCI Express, sending many packets that each write 64 bytes yields effective bandwidth well below the theoretical figure. What is the main reason?
choices: 64-byte payloads cannot be sent over PCI Express
Each packet carries headers, error-detection codes and other overhead, which are large relative to the data
Small packets are always corrupted and resent every time
io-interface-048.explanation: Besides data, a PCI Express packet carries a header with address and type, a data-link sequence number and CRC, physical-layer framing and so on, about 20 to 30 bytes in total. With 64 bytes of data, roughly 30% of the bits sent are not data. Transfers of 256 bytes or more shrink this share. This is another reason to watch packet size, not just raw bandwidth.
choiceNotes: 64 bytes can be sent without problems.
Correct. Larger packets are more efficient.
Small packets are not more error-prone.

io-interface-049.question: Which statement is correct about DMA using a ring of descriptors in memory, as widely used by network cards and NVMe SSDs?
choices: The CPU transfers data by writing it byte by byte into device registers
The CPU only writes addresses and lengths into descriptors and notifies the device, which reads them and carries out the transfers itself
Descriptors exist only inside the device and are invisible to the CPU
io-interface-049.explanation: A descriptor ring is a table in main memory, used in a circular way, where each entry says which address to transfer and how many bytes. The CPU fills free descriptors and tells the device once, through a register, how far it has written. The device reads the descriptors by DMA, transfers the data and marks finished descriptors as complete. CPU and device can advance many transfers without waiting for each other.
choiceNotes: That is programmed I/O without DMA.
Correct. Many transfers can be handed to the device at once.
Descriptors live in main memory, read and written by both CPU and device.

io-interface-050.question: Which statement is correct about PCI Express link power saving (the L0s and L1 states of ASPM)?
choices: The link enters a low-power state while idle, but returning takes time and can add latency
It raises link speed and increases power consumption
Even in the low-power state, data transfer speed is completely unaffected
io-interface-050.explanation: A SerDes consumes power to keep the link alive even when no data is flowing. With ASPM, after a period of inactivity the link enters low-power states called L0s or L1, shutting down parts of the transmit and receive circuits. L1 saves more power but takes longer to exit. Laptops use it to extend battery life, while latency-sensitive servers sometimes turn it off.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is configured by balancing power against responsiveness.
It is a power-saving feature.
The first transfer is delayed by the wake-up time.
